chunks: Determining state of charge and why it's hard. The question: How can you determine the state of charge (SoC)? Why is this often so difficult?
State of charge (SoC) is how full a battery is, as a percentage.
No sensor reads it directly, so a device has to estimate it from things it can measure: voltage, current and temperature.
Each method has a weakness, so real battery gauges combine them.
Imagine a water tank you cannot see into.
One option is a float that shows the level, but on this tank the float barely moves through the middle, and it jiggles whenever water is flowing.
The other option is to count every bucket poured in and out. That works while water flows, but a small counting mistake adds up day after day.
Combining the float and the bucket count gives a better answer than either alone.
The same 10 millivolts voltage error causes the biggest SoC error in the flat 30 to 70 % region (about 1. 3 to 2 %, worst near 40 %) and the smallest near the steep ends.
This is why voltage-only gauges are fine near empty and very uncertain mid-pack. Values come from a typical graphite/NMC OCV table.
Open-circuit voltage (OCV): the cell's voltage when it has rested with no current, which maps to SoC ("LiPo cell voltage range and why").
Voltage curve: the graph of OCV against SoC. In the middle it is very flat, about 6 millivolts per 1% of charge.
Coulomb counting: adding up current over time to track charge in and out. Drift: a small measurement error that grows over time as it accumulates.
Internal resistance: it makes voltage sag under load, which confuses a voltage-based guess ("Battery internal resistance").
Take a 2 Ah cell. A current sensor that wrongly reads 10 milliamps too high adds an error of 0. 010 times 24 equals 0. 24 Ah in one day. That is 0.
24 / 2 = 12% of the battery's capacity. Now try the voltage method. A 10 millivolts measurement error at 6 millivolts per 1% is about 1. 7% SoC.
Pull 1 amps through 100 milliohms and the sag alone is 0. 1 volts, which would fool the guess by about 17%. That is the whole idea.
"SoC can't be measured directly, only estimated.
Voltage lookup uses the open-circuit voltage curve, but that curve is flat, about 6 millivolts per percent, and it sags by I R under load.

Coulomb counting integrates current and works under load, but sensor offset accumulates, 10 milliamps on a 2 amp-hour cell is about 12 percent per day, and it needs a starting point and the correct capacity.
So gauges fuse them with a Kalman filter or impedance tracking, and correct at rest and at full or empty. The difficulty is flat curves, load, temperature, hysteresis and aging."
